phases.note: Jazz histories place swing’s rise and mainstream popularity in the 1930s, with a broad heyday from the mid-1930s to mid-1940s; the phase boundary is approximate.

nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. popular-music visibility: the Library of Congress and Philadelphia jazz histories place swing and the big-band era at the center of popular music from the 1930s into the mid-1940s. Swing continued as a practice after its period of national dominance; these are not worldwide measurements.

nodes.name: Synth-pop
nodes.description: Pop-oriented electronic music in which synthesizers and electronic production are prominent, alongside voices, guitars, drums, and other instruments. The style emerged across several scenes in the late 1970s and early 1980s; Kraftwerk and British new wave acts were influential, but neither alone defines it.
nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial shading for a short, concentrated prominence window. The dates follow this graph’s estimated period; they are not measured popularity data, and the exact boundaries need source-level review.

nodes.name: Synthwave
nodes.description: An internet-mediated electronic genre reimagining 1980s film scores, synth-pop, game music and electronic production through nostalgic, cinematic synth textures. It emerged in the mid-2000s and gained visibility in the early 2010s.

phases.note: The 2011 Drive soundtrack is used as a visibility marker in the node’s editorial chronology; the cited study addresses synthwave’s shared aesthetic and nostalgia, not a measured popularity peak.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial estimate of online-community growth and broader public visibility: synthwave formed online in the mid-to-late 2000s, with a marked visibility boost around Drive (2011), then diversified into continuing scenes. This is not a popularity ranking; global audience measures are unavailable.

nodes.name: Tango
nodes.description: A music-and-dance tradition that developed around the Río de la Plata, especially Buenos Aires and Montevideo, with African, European and local histories that should not be reduced to a single origin story.

phases.note: Circa 1880 is an editorial estimate for the emergence of tango in the Río de la Plata.
A 1914 U.S. dance manual documents international circulation by then.

nodes.phaseNote: The Río de la Plata origins are documented, while the circa-1880 anchor has low confidence as a precise boundary. A 1914 dance manual gives a medium-confidence marker for established international circulation.

nodes.name: Tech house
nodes.description: A club style combining house grooves and arrangements with techno’s stripped-down timbres and repetition; borders with minimal techno and progressive house shift across scenes.
nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial staging of emergence, the defining prominence wave, and later niche status. Boundaries are approximate and not a measured ranking; the source record should be checked for each transition.

nodes.name: Techno
nodes.description: A family of electronic dance music first named and codified around Detroit in the mid-1980s, then developed through distinct scenes across the world. Repetitive machine rhythms and studio production are common reference points, while sound and social context vary widely.
nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial staging of emergence, a defining recognition wave, and continuing activity in the current graph snapshot. These broad markers are not measured popularity data; source-level review remains needed.

nodes.name: Thrash metal
nodes.description: A fast, aggressive heavy-metal branch that sharpened riffing and rhythmic precision; the “Big Four” are Metallica, Slayer, Megadeth and Anthrax.
nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial shading for a short, concentrated prominence window. The dates follow this graph’s estimated period; they are not measured popularity data, and the exact boundaries need source-level review.

nodes.name: Trance
nodes.description: A family of electronic dance music styles built around sustained rhythmic motion and extended, often melodic development. Early German scenes, including Frankfurt, were important to its formation, alongside wider European club networks.

phases.note: Dance 2 Trance formed in Frankfurt around this time, one marker for the early European club scene.
Robert Miles’s “Children” reached number two in the UK, documenting commercial crossover in that market.

nodes.phaseNote: Medium confidence for both phase anchors. Frankfurt activity around 1990 marks early formation. The 1996 UK chart milestone marks crossover in one market. Later trance releases continued to chart.

nodes.name: Trap rap
nodes.description: A Southern US hip-hop style associated with stark programmed drums, heavy low end and narratives rooted in Atlanta trap culture; later usage broadened considerably.
nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial staging of emergence, a defining recognition wave, and continuing activity in the current graph snapshot. These broad markers are not measured popularity data; source-level review remains needed.

nodes.name: Trip-hop
nodes.description: A press-coined label for downtempo, sample-based, jazz-, funk- and soul-inflected experimental breakbeat music associated with 1990s UK scenes. The Bristol Sound is related but not identical; Massive Attack, Portishead and Tricky have rejected the trip-hop label.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate UK press, album and critical visibility: the label spread in 1994–95 around landmark Bristol releases, and the mid-1990s were its clearest commercial/cultural moment. The label remained in use as artists moved on; the profile is not a measure of the Bristol scene or worldwide listening.

nodes.name: UK garage
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate UK chart and club visibility: scene growth in the mid-1990s, chart breakthrough around the turn of the millennium, and later revival waves are documented by charts and specialist histories. These intervals describe UK visibility, not the genre’s worldwide popularity or the persistence of its underground scenes.
nodes.description: A London-centered dance style that developed in the mid-1990s from circulating US garage records and UK club, pirate-radio, and rave practices. Speed garage and 2-step brought different rhythms and production choices; later branches include grime and dubstep, without making them interchangeable genres.

nodes.name: Vaporwave
nodes.description: An internet-born music and visual culture using slowed, looped and transformed samples—often commercial, lounge and corporate soundtrack material—to engage with consumerism, nostalgia and digital circulation.

phases.note: This marks an early internet-release and forum phase; the genre label and community developed across multiple online works, so the year is approximate.
The early-2010s viral moment is often associated with 2012–14; 2012 is an approximate marker for visibility, not a single origin event.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial outline of online genre visibility: vaporwave emerged through internet releases and forums in the early 2010s, with a rapid viral/cultural moment around 2012–14, then continued in smaller, evolving communities. Not a measure of sales or all online activity.

nodes.name: Vocal jazz
nodes.description: Jazz singing that treats standards as material for interpretation, rhythmic phrasing and improvisation, rather than simply presenting a fixed popular-song performance. It spans big-band vocalists, small-group singers and later generations.
nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial staging of emergence, a defining recognition wave, and continuing activity in the current graph snapshot. These broad markers are not measured popularity data; source-level review remains needed.

nodes.name: West Coast rap
nodes.description: A regional family of styles associated with California and the wider western United States, including gangsta rap, G-funk and later Bay Area movements. Its sound and subject matter have never been uniform.
nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial staging of emergence, a defining recognition wave, and continuing activity in the current graph snapshot. These broad markers are not measured popularity data; source-level review remains needed.

nodes.name: Accordion
nodes.description: Bellows-driven free-reed instrument patented in Vienna in 1829; carried by migrants worldwide, it anchors Colombian cumbia, Dominican merengue típico, and Russian folk music.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. Its manufacture and spread across folk, dance, and popular traditions support a broad adoption-to-continuity outline. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Auto-Tune
nodes.description: Pitch-correction software released by Antares in 1997; pushed to extreme settings, from Cher's "Believe" to trap and Afrobeats, it became a deliberate vocal effect.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. Commercial release, early hit use, and later routine/creative studio use anchor the broad transitions. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Balalaika
nodes.description: Three-stringed Russian folk lute documented in writing in 1688; Vasily Andreyev and collaborators standardized concert forms and organized balalaika ensembles in the late 19th century.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The documented folk instrument and later concert standardization support a distinction between early use and organized concert visibility. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Bandoneon
nodes.description: A square, button-operated free-reed instrument developed in Germany and associated with Heinrich Band. It became a mainstay of tango ensembles in the Río de la Plata.

phases.note: Around the mid-1850s, the Band family applied a distinct name to a recognizable free-reed design.
An approximate marker for early twentieth-century adoption in tango ensembles.

nodes.phaseNote: Medium confidence for both approximate anchors. The first tracks the named German design and the second tracks its adoption in Río de la Plata tango.

nodes.name: Banjo
nodes.description: Gourd-bodied lutes made by enslaved Africans in the Caribbean, documented from the late 17th century, evolved into the commercial five-string banjo of 19th-century America and the rolling drive of bluegrass.

phases.note: Nineteenth-century commercial production and the instrument’s role in minstrel shows support this approximate expansion marker.

nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading: the banjo peaks with 19th-century minstrel and parlour music and early jazz, then continues mainly through old-time and bluegrass. Not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Bansuri
nodes.description: Side-blown bamboo flute with long-standing South Asian roots; the modern concert bansuri was developed into a solo instrument for Hindustani classical performance in the mid-20th century.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The dates follow the modern concert bansuri’s development and later establishment as a Hindustani solo instrument. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Bassoon
nodes.description: Low double-reed woodwind developed from the dulcian; its multi-jointed form emerged in the second half of the 17th century and became a bass voice in orchestras and continuo groups.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The phases reflect its emergence from earlier double-reed instruments and its consolidation in orchestral repertory. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Bongos
nodes.description: Pair of small, open-bottomed drums developed in eastern Cuba from African-derived drum traditions and closely associated with son and later salsa ensembles.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. Cuban son and later Latin jazz/salsa expansion anchor the 20th-century use markers. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Cello
nodes.description: Bowed bass instrument of the violin family, represented by surviving Cremonese examples from the mid-16th century; it became a central solo and ensemble voice in Western classical music.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The phases reflect early instrument formation, solo/ensemble expansion, and continuing orchestral and chamber use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Charango
nodes.description: A small fretted Andean lute shaped through Indigenous and Spanish instrument-making traditions, known in the Andes by the early 18th century. It is a bright rhythmic and melodic voice in Andean folk music.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The Andean instrument remains in use; the later marker reflects modern folkloric and Nueva Canción visibility rather than an origin date. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Clarinet
nodes.description: Single-reed woodwind developed from the chalumeau around 1700 by Johann Christoph Denner's workshop; a Mozart favourite and the lead voice of early New Orleans jazz and swing.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The phases reflect its early-18th-century development, classical orchestral adoption, and later popular/jazz use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Claves
nodes.description: Pair of hardwood sticks struck together; Cuban sources place their use in Havana by the 16th–17th centuries, and the clave pattern is foundational in son, rumba, and salsa.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The instrument has long-standing Cuban use; the later marker indicates prominent place in recorded Afro-Cuban and salsa ensembles. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Conga
nodes.description: Tall, single-headed Afro-Cuban drum (tumbadora) that took shape around the turn of the 20th century; it moved from rumba into son, mambo, salsa, and Latin jazz.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. Afro-Cuban rumba and later mambo/salsa circulation anchor the main shifts in recorded and performed use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Dobro resonator guitar
nodes.description: Trade-name resonator guitar introduced by the Dopyera brothers’ Dobro Manufacturing Company in 1928; its amplified projection made it influential in country and bluegrass playing.

phases.note: The Dobro Manufacturing Company was formed in 1928. The Smithsonian’s surviving Dobro instrument record dates the object later (1933–37), so this phase marks the commercial form’s company history, not a dated surviving specimen.

nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The 1928 commercial form and its subsequent country and bluegrass use anchor the broad phases. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Double bass
nodes.description: The largest bowed string instrument, descended from the violone; the low foundation of the orchestra and, plucked, the walking-bass pulse of jazz, early rock and roll, and bluegrass.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. Orchestral establishment and the later prominence of plucked walking bass in jazz anchor these markers. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Drum kit
nodes.description: Bass drum pedals of the 1900s let one player cover several drums and cymbals; the "trap kit" of early jazz grew into the backbeat engine of swing, rock and roll, funk, Afrobeat, and metal.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The phases reflect consolidation of the multi-drum kit, the swing-era prominence, and its continuing central role in popular music. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Electric bass
nodes.description: Fretted, amplified bass introduced as the Fender Precision Bass in 1951; it replaced the upright in most popular music and drives the grooves of soul, funk, reggae, and disco.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. Commercial introduction, 1960s uptake, and later standard use in popular ensembles anchor the broad shifts. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Electric guitar
nodes.description: Guitar amplified through magnetic pickups, from Rickenbacker's 1932 "Frying Pan" to the Fender and Gibson solid bodies of the early 1950s; its volume and distortion defined electric blues, rock, and metal.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The phases reflect early commercial models, postwar mass adoption, and continuing use across popular genres. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Electric piano
nodes.description: Struck tines and reeds picked up electrically, from the Wurlitzer of the mid-1950s to the Fender Rhodes of 1965; its bell-like chords colour jazz fusion, soul, and neo-soul.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The markers follow mid-century adoption, the 1960s–70s Rhodes/Wurlitzer prominence, and later continued use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: French horn
nodes.description: Coiled brass orchestral horn developed from European hunting horns; the familiar hoop form emerged in 17th-century France and was used in compositions by 1664.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The outline reflects the horn’s orchestral development and continuing use; it does not imply a single global popularity peak. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Güiro
nodes.description: Scraped idiophone traditionally made from a ridged gourd and of pre-Columbian Taíno origin. A reported late-18th-century textual reference is uncertain; the date is a provisional documentation anchor, not the instrument’s origin.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. Long-standing regional use and later prominence in Latin dance ensembles anchor a cautious outline. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Guitar
nodes.description: Waisted, fretted plucked instrument that grew from Renaissance four-course guitars into the six-string form standardised by Antonio de Torres in 19th-century Spain; the everyday accompaniment of blues, folk, country, and bossa nova.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline reflects the Renaissance form, 19th-century standardization and expansion, then broad modern use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Hammond organ
nodes.description: Electric tonewheel organ launched in 1935 as an affordable substitute for pipe organs; its growl through a Leslie speaker became a signature of soul jazz, R&B, reggae, and progressive rock.

phases.note: Hammond reports that production of the classic B-3 ended in 1975. This supports the manufacturing milestone; the broader “established” phase should not be read as a popularity measurement.

nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading: the Hammond peaks from soul jazz to late-1960s rock; tonewheel production ended in 1975 as synthesizers spread. Not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Harmonica
nodes.description: Pocket-sized free-reed instrument developed in 1820s Germany and mass-produced by Hohner; bent notes made it the wailing second voice of blues, folk, and country.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. Blues recording and later folk, country, and popular use anchor the broad prominence shifts. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Harmonium
nodes.description: A free-reed keyboard instrument adapted in South Asia as a portable, hand-pumped accompaniment. It became a defining melodic support in qawwali ensembles and other vocal traditions.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The phases reflect invention in Europe and its subsequent adaptation and establishment in South Asian devotional and classical performance. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Harp
nodes.description: A plucked-string instrument with ancient forms; arched harps are attested in the ancient Near East, and frame harps appear in medieval Europe. The timeline anchor uses the documented European frame-harp form within the graph’s supported date range.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. A continuous phase is used because the node covers many distinct harp traditions with no defensible single global prominence curve. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Harpsichord
nodes.description: Keyboard instrument that plucks its strings with quills, first documented around 1400; the continuo heart of Baroque music before the piano displaced it, then revived in the 20th century.

phases.note: A broad historical marker: the piano had largely displaced the harpsichord by around 1800 in many European contexts; later revival and continued performance mean this is not a global end date.
The Met documents the instrument’s twentieth-century revival in historically informed performance. The start is an approximate marker for that revival.

nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading: the harpsichord peaks in the Baroque continuo era, is largely eclipsed by the piano around 1800, and returns with the 20th-century revival. Not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Hichiriki
nodes.description: Small double-reed instrument with a strong, penetrating tone; a principal melody instrument in Japanese gagaku court ensembles.

phases.note: Japan Arts Council documents this instrument in gagaku kangen, an ensemble tradition transmitted for over a millennium. The start approximates early court use.

nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. A continuous phase reflects its sustained role in gagaku; the graph’s date is a broad timeline anchor, not a claimed invention date. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Jinghu
nodes.description: Small, high-pitched bowed spike fiddle and principal melodic instrument of Peking opera; extant museum examples document its 19th-century form.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The phases reflect its association with Peking opera and continuing use in that performance tradition. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Koto
nodes.description: Long Japanese zither with movable bridges, introduced from Tang China around the 8th century; first heard in the gagaku court orchestra before developing its own solo and chamber repertoire.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline reflects court use, later development of solo and ensemble repertories, and continuing practice; exact boundaries are broad. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Lute
nodes.description: Pear-shaped, fretted plucked instrument that reached Europe from the Arabic oud through Moorish Spain and Sicily, becoming the leading solo and song-accompaniment instrument of Renaissance courts.
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading: the lute peaks in the 16th century, fades as keyboards and the guitar take over in the late 18th century, and returns through the 20th-century early-music revival. Not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Mandolin
nodes.description: Small, steel-strung lute developed by the Vinaccia family of Naples in the mid-18th century; Bill Monroe made its chopped off-beat and fast tremolo central to bluegrass.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The markers reflect its Neapolitan development, 19th-century popularity, and continuing folk and popular use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Maracas
nodes.description: Seed-filled rattles with Indigenous American and African-diasporic histories; early colonial accounts document Taíno gourd rattles. The 16th-century timeline anchor records colonial-era documentation, not the instrument’s origin.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. A continuous phase avoids flattening distinct Indigenous and Afro-diasporic maraca traditions into one popularity curve. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Minimoog
nodes.description: Moog's 1970 portable, pre-wired synthesizer put the modular sound on stage; its fat lead and bass lines run through prog, funk, jazz fusion, and G-funk.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline follows its launch, rapid adoption as a portable performance synthesizer, and continuing influence. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Modular synthesizer
nodes.description: Voltage-controlled oscillators, filters, and envelopes patched together by cable, introduced by Robert Moog and Don Buchla in 1964; the sound source of early electronic, krautrock, and progressive rock records.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The outline follows early systems, wider use in electronic and experimental music, and continued studio practice. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Oboe
nodes.description: Double-reed woodwind that developed from the shawm in mid-17th-century France and entered court and orchestral music.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The phases reflect its mid-17th-century development, orchestral adoption, and continuing ensemble role. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Pedal steel guitar
nodes.description: Horizontally played steel guitar with pedals that change string pitch. Its non-pedal predecessors developed in Hawai‘i; pedal-operated models emerged around 1940 and became a defining country instrument.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. Country Hall of Fame and Smithsonian histories support the postwar adoption and continuing country use markers. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Piano
nodes.description: Bartolomeo Cristofori's hammer-action keyboard of around 1700 could play both soft and loud; it became the central instrument of Classical and Romantic music, stride and bebop jazz, and rock and roll.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline follows the early instrument, 19th-century growth into a central domestic and concert instrument, and continuing use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Pipe organ
nodes.description: Keyboard instrument sounding air through pipes; the organ returned to western Europe in the 8th century and became central to church, court, and concert music. Organ traditions elsewhere have separate histories.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The long history and varied religious, civic, and concert roles do not support a single global peak; phases are broad markers only. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Quena
nodes.description: An end-blown Andean flute with deep pre-Columbian roots; sixteenth-century accounts document Indigenous Andean flutes, while the quena remains a prominent voice in Andean folk and nueva canción.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. Longstanding Andean use continues; the later marker reflects renewed international visibility through folk revival movements. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Recorder
nodes.description: Duct flute with a thumb hole, documented in Europe from the 14th century; prized in Renaissance consorts and Baroque sonatas, it faded with the transverse flute and was revived in the 20th century.
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading: the recorder peaks in Renaissance consorts, gives way to the transverse flute in the mid-18th century, and returns with the 20th-century early-music and school revival. Not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Ryūteki
nodes.description: Side-blown bamboo flute used in Japanese gagaku; it carries a high melodic line in court dance and orchestral repertories.

phases.note: Japan Arts Council documents this instrument in gagaku kangen, an ensemble tradition transmitted for over a millennium. The start approximates early court use.

nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. A continuous phase reflects its continuing function in gagaku ensembles rather than an assumed prominence cycle. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Sampler
nodes.description: Instruments that record and replay sound, from the Fairlight CMI of 1979 to the Akai MPC of 1988; chopped breaks and loops built hip-hop, jungle, big beat, and trip-hop.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The markers follow early commercial digital sampling, hip-hop/electronic adoption, and continued production use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Sarod
nodes.description: A fretless, plucked North Indian lute that took shape from the Afghan rubab in the early 19th century. Its sustained, sliding notes became a major voice in Hindustani instrumental music.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The phases reflect the modern instrument’s formation and its continuing role in Hindustani classical performance. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Saxophone
nodes.description: Adolphe Sax's 1846 patent paired a single-reed mouthpiece with a conical metal body; it became the defining voice of jazz from swing and bebop to free jazz, and of R&B.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline follows the instrument’s development, jazz-era prominence, and continuing use in jazz and other genres. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Shō
nodes.description: Japanese free-reed mouth organ, modeled on the Chinese sheng and central to the wind section of gagaku court music.

phases.note: Japan Arts Council documents this instrument in gagaku kangen, an ensemble tradition transmitted for over a millennium. The start approximates early court use.

nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. A continuous phase reflects its sustained gagaku role; the chronology is a broad graph anchor. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Sitar
nodes.description: Long-necked lute with movable frets and sympathetic strings that took shape in 18th-century North India; Ravi Shankar carried it to global audiences and into 1960s psychedelic rock.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline reflects its modern North Indian form, mid-20th-century classical prominence, and international visibility after the 1960s. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Steelpan
nodes.description: Tuned percussion hammered from oil drums in Trinidad in the late 1930s and 1940s; steel bands became central to calypso and Carnival music.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The markers follow the instrument’s Trinidadian development, postwar steelband growth, and continuing cultural role. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Tabla
nodes.description: Pair of tuned hand drums that emerged in 18th-century North India; its spoken syllables and complex cycles accompany Hindustani classical music and qawwali.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline reflects the instrument’s modern historical formation, later concert and recording prominence, and continuing classical use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Tanpura
nodes.description: Long-necked, fretless drone lute that sustains the tonic and related pitches through South Asian classical performance; a 17th-century treatise provides early textual documentation.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. A continuous phase reflects its sustaining role across South Asian classical performance, not a popularity curve. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Roland TB-303
nodes.description: Roland launched the TB-303 bass synthesizer in 1981. Phuture’s manipulation of its resonant filter helped establish the signature sound of acid house.

phases.note: Roland dates the product launch to 1981.
Phuture’s Trax release provides a public milestone after earlier Chicago tape circulation.

nodes.phaseNote: High confidence in the manufacturer’s 1981 launch year. Medium confidence in 1987 as an adoption anchor. Club use preceded the commercial release.

nodes.name: Theremin
nodes.description: Electronic instrument played without touch, invented by Leon Theremin in 1920; its eerie glissandi featured in concert works and 1950s sci-fi films, then in the occasional rock record.
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading: the theremin peaks with mid-century film scores, fades as synthesizers spread, and returns with 1990s kit instruments. Not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Timbales
nodes.description: A pair of shallow, single-headed metal drums adapted in Cuba from 19th-century kettledrums. Their portable form developed in charanga ensembles around the turn of the 20th century and became a signature sound in salsa and Latin jazz.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The markers follow Cuban charanga and later mambo/salsa ensemble visibility, with continuing use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Roland TR-808
nodes.description: Roland launched the TR-808 analog drum machine in 1980. Its programmable sounds featured on early electro and hip-hop recordings, including “Planet Rock.”

phases.note: Roland dates the launch to 1980.
Arthur Baker used the TR-808 on “Planet Rock,” which charted in 1982.

nodes.phaseNote: High confidence in the manufacturer’s launch year. Medium confidence in the later date as a phase boundary because it is anchored to a documented recording.

nodes.name: Roland TR-909
nodes.description: Roland launched the TR-909 in 1983. It combined analog drum synthesis with sampled cymbals and became prominent in house and techno production.

phases.note: Roland dates the launch to 1983.
Roland documents the TR-909 on Derrick May’s “Strings of Life,” released in 1987.

nodes.phaseNote: High confidence in the manufacturer’s launch year. Medium confidence in the later date as a phase boundary because it is anchored to a documented recording.

nodes.name: Transverse flute
nodes.description: Side-blown flute; this entry follows the European baroque traverso developed by Paris makers in the late 17th century. Earlier transverse flutes existed in Europe and other traditions.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The phases follow the Baroque traverso, later orchestral standardization, and continuing performance use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Trombone
nodes.description: Slide brass instrument that appeared in 15th-century Burgundy as the sackbut; it accompanied Renaissance church choirs and later supplied the tailgate and riff lines of jazz and ska horn sections.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline reflects sackbut origins, later orchestral development, and continuing orchestral, jazz, and popular use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Valved trumpet
nodes.description: Valves patented by Stölzel and Blühmel in 1818 let the old natural trumpet play every chromatic note; the result became the lead horn of jazz, from Louis Armstrong to Miles Davis.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline follows the valved form, early-to-mid-20th-century jazz prominence, and continuing broad use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Tuba
nodes.description: Valved bass brass instrument patented in Prussia in 1835; the bass of the Romantic orchestra and brass bands, and the bass line of early New Orleans jazz before the string bass.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline follows its 19th-century invention, orchestral and band adoption, and continuing ensemble use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Turntables
nodes.description: Record players used as instruments: DJ Kool Herc's extended breaks in 1973 Bronx parties led to scratching and beat juggling, the founding techniques of hip-hop DJing.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The markers follow early hip-hop DJ techniques, later turntablism prominence, and continuing performance use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Vibraphone
nodes.description: Metal-barred mallet instrument with motor-driven resonator vibrato, introduced by the Leedy company in the early 1920s; jazz swing and bebop players made it a lead voice.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. Swing and bebop-era adoption anchor the main prominence marker; it remains in jazz and other ensemble settings. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Viola
nodes.description: Middle-register bowed member of the violin family, documented in northern Italy in the first half of the 16th century and used in chamber and orchestral music.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The phases reflect Renaissance-era development, orchestral/chamber consolidation, and continuing ensemble use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: Violin
nodes.description: Four-string bowed instrument shaped by northern Italian makers from Andrea Amati to Stradivari; the core of the orchestra, and as the fiddle, a lead voice in bluegrass and country.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The outline reflects Renaissance form development, Baroque/classical orchestral prominence, and continuing global use. Editorial shading only, not a measured popularity ranking; the transition years are approximate.

nodes.name: 4AD
nodes.description: British independent label founded in London in 1980; its catalogue includes influential alternative acts such as the Pixies.

nodes.name: Atlantic Records
nodes.description: New York-founded label whose long history spans blues, jazz, soul, rock and pop, including artists such as Aretha Franklin and John Coltrane.

nodes.name: Blue Note Records
nodes.description: New York jazz label founded by Alfred Lion, whose recording program documented successive currents from boogie-woogie and early jazz through bebop, hard bop, and later styles.

nodes.name: Cash Money Records
nodes.description: New Orleans label founded by brothers Bryan “Birdman” and Ronald “Slim” Williams, later home to artists including Lil Wayne.

nodes.name: Chess Records
nodes.description: Chicago record label founded by Leonard and Phil Chess; its blues and R&B catalogue includes recordings by Muddy Waters and Chuck Berry.

nodes.name: Columbia Records
nodes.description: American record label organized in Washington, D.C., in 1888 and incorporated in 1889. Its later history involved a Bridgeport manufacturing plant and a major recording operation in New York.

nodes.name: Crydamoure
nodes.description: French electronic label co-founded by Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo and Éric Chedeville, closely associated with the French Touch network.

nodes.name: Death Row Records
nodes.description: Los Angeles-area label founded in 1991 by Suge Knight, Dr. Dre and others; central to a major early-1990s West Coast rap catalogue.

nodes.name: Def Jam Recordings
nodes.description: New York label founded by Rick Rubin and Russell Simmons, initially built around emerging hip-hop and punk-informed independent practice; its roster later spanned multiple popular music styles.

nodes.name: ECM Records
nodes.description: Munich independent label founded by Manfred Eicher in 1969, with catalogues spanning jazz, improvised music and contemporary composition.

nodes.name: Ed Banger Records
nodes.description: Paris-based electronic label founded by Pedro Winter in 2003 and closely associated with a later French Touch generation.

nodes.name: F Communications
nodes.description: French electronic label founded by Éric Morand and Laurent Garnier, an important home for French techno and house.

nodes.name: Factory Records
nodes.description: Manchester independent label associated with Joy Division, New Order, A Certain Ratio, and Happy Mondays. Its work extended beyond releasing records into visual identity, club culture, and the Haçienda; the original company became insolvent in 1992.

nodes.name: Fania Records
nodes.description: New York label founded in 1964 by Johnny Pacheco and Jerry Masucci, central to the development and international circulation of salsa.

nodes.name: Impulse! Records
nodes.description: American jazz label founded in 1961, strongly associated with John Coltrane and a broad range of adventurous jazz artists.

nodes.name: Island Records
nodes.description: Record label started by Chris Blackwell in Jamaica, initially releasing Jamaican music before expanding internationally and moving its base to London in the early 1960s.

nodes.name: Kitsuné Musique
nodes.description: Paris-based independent label and fashion/music collective founded in 2002 by Gildas Loaëc and Masaya Kuroki.

nodes.name: KMS
nodes.description: Detroit techno label founded by Kevin Saunderson. The Michigan corporation dates to 1987.

nodes.name: Kompakt
nodes.description: Cologne electronic music label and company that grew from local record-shop and producer networks in the 1990s.

nodes.name: Metroplex
nodes.description: Detroit label founded by Juan Atkins in 1985. It released Model 500’s “No UFOs,” a seminal early techno record, and helped establish the independent label network around Detroit’s first techno generation.

nodes.name: Motown Records
nodes.description: Detroit label founded by Berry Gordy as part of a Black-owned music business that developed a distinctive, highly organized soul and pop production system. The label’s roster and sound helped bring its artists to broad national and international audiences.

nodes.name: Prestige Records
nodes.description: Independent jazz label launched in 1949; its catalogue includes important recordings by Miles Davis, John Coltrane and Sonny Rollins.

nodes.name: Rock Action Records
nodes.description: Glasgow label founded by members of Mogwai, supporting Scottish and international independent artists.

nodes.name: Rotterdam Records
nodes.description: Dutch hardcore label founded by Paul Elstak in Rotterdam in the early 1990s and associated with the rise of gabber.

nodes.name: Rough Trade Records
nodes.description: Independent label and record-store network that began in London and became closely associated with post-punk and independent music.

nodes.name: Roulé
nodes.description: French electronic music label established by Thomas Bangalter, whose releases became part of the French Touch club network.

nodes.name: Ruthless Records
nodes.description: Compton-associated label founded by Eazy-E and Jerry Heller, central to the early N.W.A. catalogue.

nodes.name: Sire Records
nodes.description: Independent label founded in New York by Seymour Stein and Richard Gottehrer; its history includes punk, new wave and pop artists.

nodes.name: Soma Quality Recordings
nodes.description: Independent electronic label founded in Glasgow by Slam, with an early catalogue that included Daft Punk’s “Da Funk.”

nodes.name: Source Records
nodes.description: French label launched within Virgin France that released early work by Air and Phoenix and helped connect French electronic/pop artists to wider audiences.

nodes.name: Stax Records
nodes.description: Memphis soul label founded as Satellite Records; its artists and house band helped create a distinctive Southern soul catalogue.

nodes.name: Sub Pop
nodes.description: Seattle independent label founded by Bruce Pavitt and Jonathan Poneman. Its early releases and promotional work helped bring several Northwest bands, including Nirvana and Mudhoney, to wider attention; it did not create the scene it marketed.

nodes.name: Sun Records
nodes.description: Memphis label and studio founded by Sam Phillips, known for landmark blues, country and early rock recordings.

nodes.name: Transmat
nodes.description: Detroit techno label established by Derrick May in 1986. Its early catalog includes Rhythim Is Rhythim’s “Strings of Life.”

nodes.name: Trax Records
nodes.description: An early Chicago house label that grew out of Larry Sherman’s pressing business and released records by artists including Marshall Jefferson and Phuture.

nodes.name: Tresor
nodes.description: Berlin techno label founded in 1991 alongside the Tresor club. Its early releases and collaborations helped connect Berlin and Detroit techno.

nodes.name: Underground Resistance
nodes.description: Detroit record label launched by Mike Banks and Jeff Mills in 1989, alongside the collective of the same name. It issued music by a changing roster of Detroit artists and built its own distribution and community infrastructure.

nodes.name: Virgin Records
nodes.description: British label founded in London in 1972; its later roster and imprints include major French electronic acts such as Daft Punk and Air.

nodes.name: Warp Records
nodes.description: Independent label founded in Sheffield that became an important home for electronic, experimental, and later cross-genre work. Its catalog includes artists such as Aphex Twin, Autechre, and Squarepusher.

nodes.name: Women on Wax Recordings
nodes.description: Independent Detroit dance-music label founded by DJ Minx in 2001. It has released Minx’s work and music by local and international artists.

nodes.name: Yellow Productions
nodes.description: French label founded by DJs Bob Sinclar and DJ Yellow, associated with French house and club music.

nodes.name: Accra
nodes.description: Ghanaian capital and a major center in the history and continuing practice of highlife music.

nodes.name: Antofagasta
nodes.description: Northern Chilean port city where Illapu was founded in 1971.

nodes.name: Atlanta
nodes.description: Georgia city whose hip-hop scene grew through local independent tapes, radio, clubs and studios, with OutKast among its defining acts.

nodes.name: Bali
nodes.description: Indonesian island with distinct and living gamelan traditions, including gong kebyar.

nodes.name: Beijing
nodes.description: Chinese capital and a major performance center for Peking opera, including the career and legacy of Mei Lanfang.

nodes.name: Berlin
nodes.description: German city where club culture expanded after reunification and where Detroit techno circulated through record shops, clubs, labels, and artist exchanges. Berlin producers also developed distinct strands, including dub techno.

nodes.name: Bethel
nodes.description: New York town where the 1969 Woodstock Music & Art Fair took place.

nodes.name: Birmingham
nodes.description: English city where Black Sabbath formed; its industrial setting is one part of the band’s history and not a complete explanation for heavy metal.

nodes.name: Bonn
nodes.description: German city where Ludwig van Beethoven was born.

nodes.name: Brazzaville
nodes.description: Capital of the Republic of the Congo and a key city in Congolese rumba’s shared history with Kinshasa.

nodes.name: Bristol
nodes.description: English port city whose interconnected Black British, Caribbean, punk, hip-hop, and sound-system cultures shaped several generations of local music, including the Bristol sound often called trip-hop.

nodes.name: The Bronx
nodes.description: New York City borough where hip-hop first developed as a neighborhood-based culture in the 1970s, shaped by Black, Latino, and Caribbean youth.

nodes.name: Buenos Aires
nodes.description: Argentine capital and one of tango’s foundational urban centers, in a cultural region shared with Montevideo.

nodes.name: Cairo
nodes.description: Egyptian capital and major centre for Arab musical performance, scholarship and broadcasting.

nodes.name: Cali
nodes.description: Colombian city that adopted salsa as a local music and dance culture and developed distinctive styles, clubs and festivals.

nodes.name: Chennai
nodes.description: South Indian city and a major public center for Carnatic concerts, especially the annual December music season; Carnatic music has a much wider regional history.

nodes.name: Chicago
nodes.description: A center of early house music, which developed in Black gay clubs including the Warehouse on the West Loop.

nodes.name: Cologne
nodes.description: German city whose record shops, producers and labels shaped the “Sound of Cologne” and later minimal techno networks.

nodes.name: Compton
nodes.description: Los Angeles County city central to the formation of N.W.A. and the Ruthless Records story. The link identifies a major local lineage, not a claim that one city created gangsta rap.

nodes.name: Detroit
nodes.description: Michigan city and a central site in the development of techno. The history includes Black radio and club culture, local producers and independent labels, and transnational exchanges that later shaped scenes elsewhere.

nodes.name: Düsseldorf
nodes.description: A center of West German electronic music and the former home of Kraftwerk’s Kling Klang studio.

nodes.name: Durban
nodes.description: South African coastal city where gqom emerged from local dance and club culture.

nodes.name: Faisalabad
nodes.description: Pakistani city and birthplace of Qawwali singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan.

nodes.name: Frankfurt
nodes.description: German city that became a major early techno center, with clubs and DJs including Omen and Sven Väth.

nodes.name: Glasgow
nodes.description: Scottish city with a major music ecosystem and the formation point for Mogwai.

nodes.name: Goa
nodes.description: Indian coastal state whose seasonal beach-party networks and visiting DJs helped shape Goa trance; local musicians and residents are part of this history too.

nodes.name: Grenoble
nodes.description: French Alpine city and birthplace of DJ and producer Miss Kittin.

nodes.name: Hamburg
nodes.description: German port city and home of the 1678 public opera house.

nodes.name: Havana
nodes.description: Cuban capital with a deep recorded history in son, rumba and other musical traditions; many later salsa histories also connect Cuba and New York.

nodes.name: Houston
nodes.description: Texas city with a distinct hip-hop tradition; DJ Screw’s slowed, repeated mixtape production helped define chopped and screwed.

nodes.name: Jamaica
nodes.description: Caribbean island whose musical traditions include mento, ska, rocksteady, reggae, dub, and dancehall; these forms developed through local practice and transnational exchange.

nodes.name: Johannesburg
nodes.description: South African metropolis whose townships and club networks were central to the emergence of kwaito.

nodes.name: Karachi
nodes.description: Pakistani port city where the Sabri Brothers settled after Partition and formed their celebrated Qawwali partnership.

nodes.name: Kingston
nodes.description: Jamaica’s capital and a central site in the development of reggae and its sound-system culture; UNESCO identifies western Kingston as a key cultural space for reggae’s emergence.

nodes.name: Kinshasa
nodes.description: Capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and a cradle of Congolese rumba, with pioneering recording studios and bands.

nodes.name: Kushtia
nodes.description: Bangladesh district closely associated with Baul master Lalon Shah and a living Baul community; Baul practice is dispersed across rural Bangladesh and West Bengal.

nodes.name: Lagos
nodes.description: Nigerian megacity central to the late-1960s emergence and subsequent performance history of Afrobeat, including Fela Kuti’s politically engaged club and band culture.

nodes.name: Leipzig
nodes.description: German city central to Johann Sebastian Bach’s later career and musical legacy.

nodes.name: Liverpool
nodes.description: Port city whose postwar popular music scene, including the Beatles and the Cavern Club, became internationally influential.

nodes.name: London
nodes.description: A center of British acid house and rave, documented by late-1980s club flyers and scene memorabilia.

nodes.name: Los Angeles
nodes.description: Southern California music center with a major West Coast hip-hop and record-industry history.

nodes.name: Manchester
nodes.description: Northern English city whose post-punk, independent-label, club, and dance histories include Factory Records, the Haçienda, and the Madchester era.

nodes.name: Mar del Plata
nodes.description: Argentine coastal city and birthplace of composer and bandoneon player Astor Piazzolla.

nodes.name: Memphis
nodes.description: Tennessee city with a major blues, soul and rock recording history, including Sun and Stax; musicians from across the South helped shape its sound.

nodes.name: Mexico City
nodes.description: Mexican capital and metropolitan center that includes Iztapalapa, the home base of Los Ángeles Azules.

nodes.name: Minneapolis
nodes.description: Minnesota city whose studio, club and musician networks helped Prince develop the Minneapolis Sound.

nodes.name: Monterey
nodes.description: California city that hosted the 1967 Monterey International Pop Festival.

nodes.name: Montevideo
nodes.description: Uruguayan capital with a foundational role in tango’s shared Río de la Plata history alongside Buenos Aires.

nodes.name: Munich
nodes.description: German city where Manfred Eicher founded ECM Records in 1969.

nodes.name: Nashville
nodes.description: Tennessee music center whose recording, publishing and broadcast networks became central to country music; it is one hub within a broader Southern tradition.

nodes.name: New Orleans
nodes.description: Louisiana port city whose African American musical communities and distinctive cultural history were central to early jazz.

nodes.name: New York
nodes.description: The Bronx was an early center of hip-hop, and Manhattan clubs such as Paradise Garage helped shape dance-floor culture.

nodes.name: Oakland
nodes.description: California city within the wider San Francisco Bay Area, strongly associated with hyphy and Bay Area rap.

nodes.name: Paris
nodes.description: French capital and a central meeting, club and label hub for the French Touch. The movement developed through overlapping Paris and Versailles networks.

nodes.name: Port of Spain
nodes.description: Trinidad and Tobago’s capital and a major center for calypso; the tradition is rooted across Trinidad and the wider Caribbean.

nodes.name: Pretoria
nodes.description: South African capital and one of the Gauteng centers in the early development of amapiano.

nodes.name: Rio de Janeiro
nodes.description: Brazilian city where bossa nova emerged in the late 1950s through musicians combining samba-based practice with jazz and new approaches to guitar, harmony, and song.

nodes.name: Rotterdam
nodes.description: Dutch port city where the early gabber scene developed through clubs, record shops, parties and independent labels.

nodes.name: Salvador
nodes.description: Brazilian coastal city and birthplace of singer-songwriter Dorival Caymmi, whose work drew deeply on Bahia.

nodes.name: Salzburg
nodes.description: Austrian city where Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born and grew up.

nodes.name: San Francisco
nodes.description: California city and an important center of the 1960s psychedelic rock counterculture, including the Haight-Ashbury scene.

nodes.name: San Juan
nodes.description: Puerto Rico’s capital and a major center for reggaeton’s development and international circulation.

nodes.name: Santiago
nodes.description: Chile’s capital and a major gathering point for Nueva Canción and related folk-protest movements, with roots beyond the city.

nodes.name: Santo Domingo
nodes.description: Capital of the Dominican Republic and a key merengue center, associated with Juan Luis Guerra’s musical career.

nodes.name: Seattle
nodes.description: Pacific Northwest city with a long-standing local music network; its 1980s underground rock scene became internationally associated with grunge, while Sub Pop helped circulate some of its groups.

nodes.name: Seoul
nodes.description: South Korean capital and a central production, management and media hub for contemporary K-pop.

nodes.name: Sheffield
nodes.description: Northern English city where Warp Records was founded in 1989; the label later developed an international catalog across electronic and experimental music.

nodes.name: Southwest Korea
nodes.description: A broad region identified by UNESCO as the historical home of pansori’s emergence.

nodes.name: St Petersburg
nodes.description: Russian city whose conservatory and theaters were important to the musical education and careers of several Russian composers.

nodes.name: Tokyo
nodes.description: Japanese capital and the home base for Pizzicato Five, one of the best-known Shibuya-kei acts.

nodes.name: Tuva
nodes.description: Republic in southern Siberia and home to living Tuvan throat-singing traditions, including xöömei.

nodes.name: Varanasi
nodes.description: North Indian city and birthplace of Ravi Shankar, whose career helped bring Hindustani classical music to international audiences.

nodes.name: Venice
nodes.description: Italian city where Antonio Vivaldi was born and worked for much of his career.

nodes.name: Versailles
nodes.description: City west of Paris whose school and friendship networks produced several central French Touch acts, including Air and Phoenix; this is a regional contribution, not an exclusive origin claim.

nodes.name: Vienna
nodes.description: Austrian capital and a major center of classical and Romantic music; composers from several countries built careers there.

nodes.name: Warsaw
nodes.description: Polish capital where Frédéric Chopin studied and launched his public career before leaving Poland.

nodes.name: Washington, D.C.
nodes.description: U.S. capital and birthplace of Duke Ellington, whose later career transformed New York’s Cotton Club and jazz scene.

nodes.name: Wigan
nodes.description: English town whose Casino became a defining venue in the British Northern Soul scene from 1973 until its closure in 1981.

nodes.name: Yogyakarta
nodes.description: Indonesian city and court center with a prominent Javanese gamelan tradition.

nodes.name: Accra highlife scene
nodes.description: A major urban hub in a transnational Ghanaian genre whose styles and performance practices developed across communities and regions.

nodes.name: Atlanta hip-hop scene
nodes.description: A locally rooted rap network shaped by independent tapes, radio, clubs and studios; its history includes OutKast, the Dungeon Family and many distinct Southern styles.

nodes.name: Balinese gamelan traditions
nodes.description: Distinct island-wide and local performance traditions, including gong kebyar, which emerged in northern Bali in the early twentieth century.

nodes.name: Baul music tradition
nodes.description: A devotional and philosophical music practice of itinerant minstrels across rural Bangladesh and West Bengal; the tradition has no single city of origin.

nodes.name: Beijing Peking opera scene
nodes.description: A performance tradition with deep roots in Beijing, associated with artists including Mei Lanfang and many other performers and companies.

nodes.name: Birmingham heavy metal scene
nodes.description: A group of Birmingham-area bands and venues that helped establish heavy metal, with Black Sabbath central to the early history.

nodes.name: Bristol sound
nodes.description: A loose, internally varied network of Bristol musicians and sound-system practitioners drawing on reggae, dub, hip-hop, punk, and electronic music. “Trip-hop” became a common outside label, while some Bristol artists preferred “Bristol sound.”

nodes.name: South Bronx hip-hop scene
nodes.description: A neighborhood-rooted cultural movement built by Black, Latino, and West Indian teenagers through DJing, MCing, dance, and visual art. Its early history is community-based and should not be reduced to a single inventor or party.

nodes.name: Cali salsa scene
nodes.description: A local salsa and dance culture shaped through radio, records, clubs, dance schools and festivals, drawing on music from across the Caribbean and diaspora.

nodes.name: CBGB
nodes.description: Manhattan club that became a crucial performance room for downtown punk, new wave, and later hardcore. Its history includes a wider range of underground music than the punk label alone suggests.

nodes.name: Chennai Carnatic music season
nodes.description: An annual December concert season in Chennai that brings together performers and audiences from a much broader Carnatic tradition.

nodes.name: Chicago blues scene
nodes.description: A city-centered electric blues network shaped by musicians who moved from the South and the independent labels and clubs of Chicago.

nodes.name: Chile Nueva Canción movement
nodes.description: A politically engaged folk movement with important networks in Santiago and across Chile and Latin America.

nodes.name: Cologne minimal techno scene
nodes.description: A Cologne electronic music network shaped by record shops, labels and producers, including Kompakt and its founders.

nodes.name: Compton hip-hop scene
nodes.description: A local hip-hop lineage associated with N.W.A. and Ruthless Records, within a much larger and varied Los Angeles-area history.

nodes.name: Congolese rumba scene
nodes.description: A shared musical history centered in Kinshasa and Brazzaville, shaped by local musicians, studios, dance bands and transnational exchange.

nodes.name: Dominican merengue scene
nodes.description: A Dominican dance-music tradition with Santo Domingo as one central recording and performance hub.

nodes.name: Durban gqom scene
nodes.description: A Durban-born dance music network that grew through local producers, DJs, clubs and informal circulation.

nodes.name: Düsseldorf krautrock scene
nodes.description: A West German experimental music network associated with Kraftwerk and other groups, part of the broader and internally diverse Krautrock history.

nodes.name: Frankfurt techno scene
nodes.description: A German techno network of clubs, DJs and labels, including Omen and Sven Väth; Frankfurt was one of several important German centers.

nodes.name: French Touch
nodes.description: Paris–Versailles electronic music network in which house, disco sampling, independent labels and club culture intersected in the 1990s and 2000s. The label is an umbrella, not a single uniform sound.

nodes.name: Gauteng amapiano scene
nodes.description: A township-rooted dance-music network associated with overlapping experimentation in Pretoria and Johannesburg; accounts of its exact point of origin remain contested.

nodes.name: Glasgow post-rock scene
nodes.description: Glasgow’s independent music network around the formation of Mogwai and the later Rock Action label.

nodes.name: Goa trance scene
nodes.description: A seasonal DJ-led psychedelic dance network that developed in Goa in dialogue with travelers, local communities and international electronic music.

nodes.name: The Haçienda
nodes.description: Manchester nightclub operated by Factory Records. It connected post-punk, Black club traditions, house, acid house, and rave culture across its fifteen-year life.

nodes.name: Havana son and salsa traditions
nodes.description: Cuban urban music traditions around son and related forms; later salsa movements connect Cuban musical roots with New York musicians and communities.

nodes.name: Houston hip-hop scene
nodes.description: A regional hip-hop ecosystem encompassing DJ Screw’s chopped-and-screwed mixtapes, the Screwed Up Click and other distinct local lineages.

nodes.name: Javanese gamelan traditions
nodes.description: Court, village and community performance traditions associated with Java, including the Yogyakarta and Surakarta regions.

nodes.name: Johannesburg kwaito scene
nodes.description: A post-apartheid dance-music movement associated with Johannesburg’s townships and club culture; its roots and practitioners are diverse.

nodes.name: Kingston reggae and sound-system culture
nodes.description: A layered Kingston-centered history of Jamaican recording, sound systems, studio practice, and performance. Reggae grew from earlier Jamaican forms and cross-border musical exchange rather than from a single venue or individual.

nodes.name: Kingston ska scene
nodes.description: A Jamaican studio and performance network associated with early ska artists including the Skatalites and Prince Buster.

nodes.name: Memphis soul and recording scene
nodes.description: A network of studios and musicians around Sun and Stax that helped shape blues, soul and early rock recordings. The sound drew on a much wider Southern musical world.

nodes.name: Merseybeat
nodes.description: Liverpool's Merseybeat boom grew from late-1950s roots, became a thriving local scene in 1961, dominated the UK charts by 1963, and had largely ended by 1965.

nodes.name: Mexican cumbia sonidera scene
nodes.description: A Mexico City sound-system and dance tradition associated with Iztapalapa and Los Ángeles Azules; cumbia itself has multiple regional histories.

nodes.name: Minneapolis Sound
nodes.description: A cross-genre studio and performance idiom associated with Prince and the musicians and venues around him in Minneapolis.

nodes.name: Music Institute
nodes.description: A Detroit after-hours club founded by George Baker, Chez Damier and Alton Miller. Its house and techno nights ran from May 1988 to November 1989.

nodes.name: Nashville country music scene
nodes.description: A recording, publishing and broadcast center for country music, built alongside regional traditions across the American South.

nodes.name: New Orleans jazz scene
nodes.description: A historically important jazz network whose musicians drew on African American, Caribbean, European and local traditions.

nodes.name: New York salsa scene
nodes.description: A New York Latin music movement shaped by Caribbean migration, Cuban musical forms and local musicians, labels and dance venues.

nodes.name: Paradise Garage
nodes.description: A New York dance club at 84 King Street with resident DJ Larry Levan and a largely Black gay following. Construction parties began in 1977, the club officially opened as Paradise Garage in 1978, and it closed in 1987.

nodes.name: Port of Spain calypso scene
nodes.description: A major calypso center within a tradition rooted in Trinidadian communities and spread across the Caribbean and diaspora.

nodes.name: Río de la Plata tango scene
nodes.description: A shared urban tradition around Buenos Aires and Montevideo, shaped by migration, dance, song and exchange across the estuary.

nodes.name: Rotterdam gabber scene
nodes.description: A Dutch hardcore network centered in Rotterdam clubs, record shops and parties; its early history includes Parkzicht, DJ Paul Elstak and Rotterdam Records.

nodes.name: San Francisco Bay Area hyphy scene
nodes.description: A Bay Area rap and dance movement associated with artists including E-40, Mac Dre and Keak da Sneak; it developed across cities and neighborhoods, not only Oakland.

nodes.name: San Francisco psychedelic scene
nodes.description: A 1960s countercultural music network around venues and neighborhoods including Haight-Ashbury, with the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane among its acts.

nodes.name: San Juan reggaeton scene
nodes.description: A Puerto Rican urban music network that helped shape reggaeton, with roots in Jamaican dancehall, Panama and local styles.

nodes.name: Seattle underground rock scene
nodes.description: A locally connected rock scene spanning independent labels, clubs, and bands whose sound drew on punk, metal, and other regional influences. “Grunge” later became a media and industry category, not a complete description of Seattle music.

nodes.name: Second Summer of Love
nodes.description: A British acid house and rave wave that spread through clubs and warehouse parties in 1988 and continued into larger events in 1989.

nodes.name: Seoul K-pop industry
nodes.description: A contemporary pop production and media ecosystem centered in Seoul, while K-pop artists and audiences are global and geographically diverse.

nodes.name: Sheffield electronic music scene
nodes.description: A city network of post-punk, synth-pop and dance music around groups such as the Human League, Cabaret Voltaire and label Warp.

nodes.name: Studio 54
nodes.description: New York discotheque whose first period made it a globally visible symbol of disco-era nightlife, celebrity culture, and DJ-centered dancing. The club’s broader venue history continued after its initial 1980 closure.

nodes.name: The Warehouse
nodes.description: A Chicago club founded by Robert Williams, with Frankie Knuckles as resident DJ. Its predominantly Black gay dance floor helped shape early house music.

nodes.name: Tokyo Shibuya-kei scene
nodes.description: A 1990s Tokyo pop network associated with eclectic sampling, indie record culture and groups such as Pizzicato Five.

nodes.name: Tuvan xöömei tradition
nodes.description: A living vocal music tradition of Tuva, practiced in multiple styles and communities; Huun-Huur-Tu is one internationally known ensemble.

nodes.name: Vienna classical music milieu
nodes.description: A historically important urban center in which composers from different backgrounds worked; not a single school or exclusive origin for classical music.

nodes.name: Wigan Casino
nodes.description: Northern Soul all-nighter venue whose dancers, DJs, and rare-soul record culture made it a defining British club scene; its importance should not be mistaken for the whole Northern Soul movement.

nodes.name: Raï
nodes.description: A popular song tradition from western Algeria, shaped by rural poetic singing and the urban culture of Oran. Cheikhas and later young singers developed its frank lyrics and, over time, incorporated electric instruments and new production styles.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. Broad markers distinguish the documented western Algerian roots, the 1970s–80s youth and recording wave, and continuing practice. Editorial shading, not a measured ranking; dates are approximate.

nodes.name: Gnawa
nodes.description: Moroccan musical and ritual practices rooted in communities whose histories include the trans-Saharan slave trade. Singing, guembri and metal castanets accompany ceremonies as well as public performances; the timeline date is an approximate anchor, not a precise origin.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. Gnawa is a living ritual and musical tradition, not a time-bounded popularity cycle; a single continuous phase avoids suggesting an invented peak. Editorial shading, not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Algerian chaâbi
nodes.description: An urban popular tradition associated with the Casbah of Algiers, shaped by Andalusian musical forms, sung poetry and musicians including El Anka. It is distinct from Moroccan styles also called chaâbi.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. Markers sketch the urban development associated with Algiers and El Anka, followed by continuing repertory and performance. Editorial shading, not a measured ranking; boundaries are approximate.

nodes.name: Mbalax
nodes.description: Senegalese urban dance music combining local vocal and sabar-drum traditions with electric bands and influences from across Africa and the Atlantic. Dakar groups and singers including Youssou N’Dour helped develop its modern sound.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. Markers sketch the 1970s emergence, 1980s expansion with Senegalese dance bands, and continuing practice. Editorial shading, not a measured ranking; boundaries are approximate.

nodes.name: Makossa
nodes.description: A Cameroonian dance-music style associated with Douala, whose modern sound developed around prominent bass, guitars and horns. Manu Dibango’s 1972 recording “Soul Makossa” carried one jazz- and soul-inflected interpretation to international audiences.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The 1970s marker reflects its international visibility, including Manu Dibango, while later phases represent continued local and diasporic practice. Editorial shading, not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Taarab
nodes.description: A Swahili coastal music tradition associated with Zanzibar and East Africa, shaped by exchanges among African, Arab and Indian Ocean cultures. Orchestras and singers including Siti binti Saad brought its songs into recordings, clubs and community celebrations.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low to medium. Markers sketch early urban orchestral growth, later recording and performance prominence, and continued practice; the tradition varies across the Swahili coast. Editorial shading, not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Youssou N’Dour

nodes.name: Thione Seck

nodes.name: Manu Dibango
